newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE: Nervous Networks Rush To Make Expensive Deals.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE: Nervous Networks Rush To Make Expensive Deals.

text.p: HOLLYWOOD (Variety) - Even though the new TV season is turning up few, if any, bonafide hits, networks are already making unprecedented commitments to producers for new shows.

Television executives are shaking their heads in disbelief at the cash they're shelling out to sign talent to new projects. To make matters worse, networks are at times committing to between six and 13 episodes rather than the usual one-off pilot.

"We are watching the inevitable outcome of the most competitive TV environment ever," says David A. Neuman, president of network TV at Walt Disney Television. "The networks are all trying to reserve resources in an effort to stay ahead of the game."
ABC, for example, has struck a 13-episode deal valued at $1.3 million per show to Universal Television for a series version of the Jean-Claude Van Damme theatrical Time Cop.
Fox Broadcasting has sealed an equally expensive pact with Universal for the period drama Roar, which some industry observers describe as Braveheart -- The Series.

The early and extensive dealmaking, says NBC Entertainment president Warren Littlefield "ultimately clogs up your opportunities. We learned a lot of lessons in the 1980s when we accelerated our decline by giving away our real estate to people who delivered in the past."
What differentiates this period from other periods, says ABC Entertainment chairman Ted Harbert, is the number of firm episodic commitments networks are making to some shows.

"What that leads to," says Harbert, "is the skipping of a crucial development step. It is an expensive and risky business to skip writing a script and shooting a pilot and instead going straight to episodes." But, he adds, "I can't blame the studios and agents for asking for this. We get what we bargain for."
"The level of commitments this early matters," adds CBS Entertainment president Les Moonves. "It hampers development a lot."

Besides Time Cop, ABC has also made multi-episode commitments to director Spike Lee and former New World Entertainment chairman Brandon Tartikoff, who are partnering on a show; She's The One director Ed Burns; "Roseanne" co-star Laurie Metcalf; and Tracy Pollan, wife of ABC's Spin City star Michael J. Fox.
CBS has a series commitment with Tom Selleck as well as pricey pilot deals with David Caruso, Ann-Margret, Valerie Bertinelli and even a development deal with author Anne Rice.
Fox is also looking to cash in on the success of Independence Day with The Visitor, an expensive spinoff.
Even NBC, whose No. 1 status in the ratings gives it more clout in negotiations for product, has a few major deals.

Friends producers Kevin Bright, Marta Kauffmann and David Crane will have a new comedy starring Kirstie Alley on the schedule next year and has episode commitments to Tony Danza and Charles Dutton, as well as plans to develop a new drama from ER executive producer John Wells.
Industry execs are quick to point out that even the heftiest of programming commitments have escape clauses.

Last year, CBS was unhappy with the show Firehouse and opted to pay the penalty rather than put it on the air. But these clauses are costly and will probably serve as a reminder to the networks as to which shows are priorities.

Spurring all these early deals, of course, is the fact that the new season is by most accounts so lackluster. While Cosby and Spin City are posting decent numbers, neither are breakout hits yet. Suddenly Susan, starring Brooke Shields loses between four and seven share points off its Seinfeld lead-in and the retooled Ink is not breaking any ratings records either.
Although all those shows were far from cheap, the networks continue to reach into seemingly bottomless wallets in hopes of landing the next hit.
While these big commitments run the risk of dampening the development season, talent agents and some studio heads counter with that in the end quality will out.
"At the end of the day the great show will get on," says one top TV agent. "We saw that with 'Ink.' CBS didn't like the show and had it done again."

Of course, the cost of retooling Ink to CBS was an additional $4 million on top of the nearly $1 million per-episode fee the network had already committed to DreamWorks, the producer of the show. As for DreamWorks, it had to cede a stake in the show to producer Diane English in return for her efforts in fixing the sitcom.
Reuters/Variety
